short: An emperor's private Stoic notebook, never meant for publication, became a classic of philosophy.
full:
While commanding campaigns against Germanic tribes along the Danube frontier in the 170s AD, Marcus Aurelius kept a private notebook of Stoic reflections, written in Greek for his own use and addressed to himself, not an audience. Drawing on Epictetus and earlier Stoic teaching, the entries return repeatedly to the same themes: the impermanence of fame and the body, duty performed without complaint, and the discipline of judging events by reason rather than appetite.

The work carried no title in antiquity and was never intended as a philosophical treatise for others; it survived by chance transmission and was first printed only in the sixteenth century, acquiring the title Meditations along the way. Its unguarded, repetitive honesty, from a man who held supreme power until his death in AD 180, has made it one of the most widely read texts of Stoic philosophy in any era.
